page: Alibaba Cloud ecs.c1.large is a compute-optimized virtual machine instance belonging to the ecs.c1 server family. It is built on the x86_64 CPU architecture and features 8 dedicated vCPUs paired with 16.0 GB of system memory, yielding a resource density of 2.0 GB of RAM per core. The instance runs on the KVM hypervisor and does not include any complimentary public IPv4 addresses.

This instance does not include any bundled local storage, meaning all storage requirements must be met via external network-attached block storage. There are no integrated GPUs, making it unsuitable for hardware-accelerated workloads. The underlying CPU allocation is dedicated, ensuring consistent processing power without resource contention from neighboring tenants.

A key technical tradeoff of the ecs.c1.large is the lack of advanced CPU instruction sets. The hardware does not support Advanced Vector Extensions (AVX, AVX512), Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX), or hardware-accelerated cryptography (AES, SHA_NI). This absence represents a significant limitation for workloads relying on vector math, machine learning inference, or intensive cryptographic operations.

From a qualitative cost-efficiency perspective, the ecs.c1.large offers a lean compute-to-memory ratio suitable for budget-conscious compute tasks that do not require specialized instruction sets or local storage. It is best suited for standard web serving, lightweight batch processing, and general-purpose compute workloads that require dedicated CPU resources but do not demand high-performance vector calculations.

It does not include bundled local storage or integrated GPUs, requiring external block storage for data persistence. A key technical tradeoff is the lack of advanced CPU instruction sets, such as AVX, AVX512, AMX, and hardware cryptography extensions, which limits its suitability for vector-heavy math or intensive encryption. Qualitatively, the instance offers a cost-effective option for dedicated compute resources. It is best suited for standard web serving, basic batch processing, and general-purpose utility workloads that require dedicated CPU allocation without the need for specialized hardware acceleration or high-performance vector instructions.
